No interim asset sale or borrowing is allowed to satisfy the design constraints. Initial cash must cover the largest design call plus grant and leave the buffer. Joint manager stress returns include stipulated residual outcomes as well as factor loadings and the annual fee. Do not average the scenarios or imply that surviving them guarantees safety.

Apply the outside-design scenario separately to the approved target. The board has authorized a contingency bond sale at date 1, before paying the call and grant, limited to 100 original units and no more than held. Each original unit is then marked at 0.98 CU. Its executable proceeds are that mark minus spread 0.020 and fee 0.002 CU per unit. Continuous original units are permitted for this emergency sale; initial 25-CU lots need not be preserved. Sell the minimum needed to restore the buffer if capacity permits. Reconcile marked value removed, costs, net cash and foregone terminal bond proceeds. No new borrowing or private sale is allowed. If scheduled payments themselves cannot be made, report failure and leave unsupported subsequent claim values undefined.

Initial execution and later reporting

The desk first attempts the approved target's bond sale. Only 75 units are executable at the 1-CU reference price, with the stated initial fee; this sale settles before any equity purchase. Test what would happen if the entire intended equity purchase were then completed. Under an ex-ante continuation rule, hold the actual post-sale bond position and intended manager position fixed, and select the best robust-score feasible initial-grid portfolio whose E holding lies between inherited and intended E. If none exists, escalate; do not silently weaken limits. Preserve all unfilled bond units and canceled equity units in the report. No equity purchase followed by an imaginary free reversal occurs.

For evaluation use the held-out compounded liquid returns, actual private final distribution 300 CU and ordinary call/grants (80/60 at date 1, 40 at date 2). The cash account still earns 1.005 per half year. Report terminal reserve for the approved target, authorized actual portfolio, strategic benchmark and nominal-policy counterfactual. Reconcile actual minus benchmark into target minus benchmark plus actual minus target. Decompose the target/actual gap into return opportunity, difference in fees carried to the terminal date and any cash-principal timing adjustment. Explain why this is a matched-wealth comparison rather than a fabricated private-asset time-weighted return. The dated return-method reference supports explicit flow and fee boundaries; no standards-compliance claim is made.

100-point criterion rubric

Six essential domains with analytic partial credit
DomainPointsCredit allocation
Evidence and information20Cutoffs, versions and eligibility 6; fees/closure/cohort reconciliation 6; complete search and held-out statistics 5; justified inference limits 3.
Risk and forecast model20Sample/prior blend and units 5; full covariance, private cross-risk and bounded consistency 6; means and total/active variance 5; ambiguity and evidence distinction 4.
Allocation and design funding20Budget, costs, grid and all constraints 5; global finite enumeration, ranking and tie rule 6; robust/nominal/benchmark schedules 6; meaningful near-boundary interpretation 3.
Execution, outside stress and report20Naive breach and authorized fallback 5; forced-sale rights/costs/dated funding 6; target/actual/benchmark and implementation identity 6; unresolved gaps and measurement limits 3.
IPS and committee judgment10Coherent conditional decision and responsibilities 4; evidence requests linked to actions 3; monitoring, escalation and benchmark discipline 3.
Reproduction and defense10Independent executable model, provenance and preserved baseline 4; meaningful checks 3; successful intervention/teach-back 3.

Advancement requires 85/100 overall, at least 15/20 in each 20-point domain and 7.5/10 in each 10-point domain, plus satisfactory transfer and teach-back. These are author-designed criteria, not an institution's requirements. Fractional credit is permitted. Carry forward a transparent arithmetic slip without repeatedly deducting for its consequences; separately score new reasoning errors. A justified alternative policy recommendation can earn full judgment credit, but it must correctly reproduce the assigned policy before changing its premises.

Critical errors require remediation irrespective of total: using future releases or held-out outcomes in January selection; concealing a failed entrant or search trial; claiming a sample intercept establishes a priced premium or skill; omitting private or cross-covariance risk; spending private accounting value as cash; counting an internal call as an external grant; funding a payment with an unavailable claim; ignoring sale fees or keeping sold bonds' terminal proceeds; presenting a buffer/floor breach as feasible; or changing the benchmark after observing performance. Require a corrected artifact, causal explanation and fresh transfer before advancement.

Complete instructor guide, benchmark and intervention answers

  1. Available information and the selected manager

    Filter each record by release date before any return calculation. The manager comparison during training is [0.014, −0.004, 0.018, 0]. K's active vector is [0.006, 0.006, 0.006, 0.006]; M's first-vintage vector is [0.004, 0, 0.002, 0.002]. K therefore wins the frozen arithmetic rule, 0.6% versus 0.2% per quarter. CX is closed; N has not entered. Keep both in the audit with different reasons for exclusion from new allocation. Complete available histories are an eligibility condition, not permission to conceal an otherwise eligible missing record.

    The later M correction replaces 0.002 with 0.026 for final reporting, adding 0.024/4 = 0.006 to its training active mean. Retrospective M mean becomes 0.008 and overtakes K. Including N's late backfill creates a still different winner with active mean 0.191. Neither reconstruction describes the January information set. The original release remains part of the trace even when a revised statistic is useful for final performance reporting.

    For returns r and comparison b, active mean is the mean of r − b; tracking-error variance is Σ[(r − b) − mean(r − b)]²/3. M's training variance is 1/375,000, tracking error about 0.001632993 per quarter and IR about 1.224745. K's variance is zero, so its IR is undefined and serialized as null. Calling it infinitely skilled confuses a degenerate sample with an economic opportunity. The four disclosed trial winners are K for mean active, K for compound relative wealth, K for last active, and M among defined sample IRs. Reporting all trials exposes the decision process; no unprovided independence assumption turns four trials into a calibrated multiplicity correction.

    The comparison regression uses slope Cov(r,b)/Var(b) and intercept mean(r) − slope × mean(b). K has slope 1, intercept 0.006 and residual squared sum 0 in just four deliberately constructed observations. M's first-vintage slope is 94/85, intercept 107/85,000 and residual squared sum 89/21,250,000. These are sample descriptions. A population alpha requires a maintained conditional return model; a priced factor premium requires a pricing restriction beyond fit; skill requires more evidence than either sample label. The committee must not set the forward overlay to four times K's fitted intercept by assertion.

    A net fee of 0.002 means 0.002 times opening wealth is paid. Subtract it before compounding; multiplying gross wealth by 0.998 would implement a different ending-base contract. K's training growth factor is 51,408,612/48,828,125; M's available-vintage factor is 3,238,359,291/3,125,000,000. CX's liquidation leaves 1.05 × 1.04 × 0.70 = 0.7644. Keeping this capital in zero-return cash gives the fourth and later periods gross factors of one, preserving the last loss and liquidation proceeds exactly.

    Training survivor-only return = (GK + GM)/2 − 1 = 278510459/6250000000 = 4.456167344%.

    The arithmetic average of terminal account factors is appropriate for equal initial allocations without rebalancing. Averaging each period's manager returns and then compounding instead describes a periodically rebalanced cohort. Dropping CX changes the population as well as the average; replacing its capital by zero would introduce an additional false loss, while restarting cash at one would erase a real loss.

  3. Risk derivation and a coherent joint law

    The E/B sample means are 0.01 and 0.005. Their centered cross products sum to 0.0052, −0.0014 and 0.0005. Dividing by three gives SEE = 13/7500, SEB = −7/15000 and SBB = 1/6000. The chosen blend is Σ = [[44/1875, 2/1875], [2/1875, 2/375]]. Its leading entry is positive and determinant is 436/3515625 > 0, so it is positive definite. The sign of its cross term differs from the small sample's because the prior contributes positive cross-covariance. No ranking success proves that the prior or intensity was well chosen.

    Write the random claim vector as H = (rE, rB, rM, DP). With loadings L = [[1,0], [0,1], [0.4,0.6], [140,40]], its covariance is LΣL′ + diag(0,0,0.0016,400). For every vector w, w′Cov(H)w = (L′w)′Σ(L′w) + 0.0016wM² + 400wP² ≥ 0. The private row/column has mixed CU-return units; the final quadratic form with positions (x,y,z,1) has units CU². This construction exposes both manager/private cross-covariances through common factors. Assuming all alternative assets are independent would discard those terms.

    For a concrete finite witness, take independent signs U1, U2, UM, UP, each ±1 with probability 1/2. Define A = √ΣEE, B = ΣEB/A and C = √(ΣBB − ΣEB²/ΣEE). Put FE = AU1, FB = BU1 + CU2, εM = 0.04UM, εP = 20UP. The 16 equally weighted states reproduce all means, variances and orthogonalities. Approximately A = 0.153188337, B = 0.006963106, C = 0.072696963. The manager deviation is bounded by 0.149071377; the private deviation by 44.63277 CU. Even the lower-overlay manager gross payoff and private payout are positive in every state. These are stipulated physical moments, not a calibrated likelihood or set of state prices; the stress register has its own conditional scope.

    u = x + 0.4z + 140; v = y + 0.6z + 40.
    V = u²ΣEE + 2uvΣEB + v²ΣBB + 0.0016z² + 400.
    p = x + 0.4z − 250; q = y + 0.6z − 300.
    Aactive = p²ΣEE + 2pqΣEB + q²ΣBB + 0.0016z².

    Private exposure and its residual disappear from active variance only because target and strategic benchmark own exactly the same claim. They remain in total risk. The limits correspond to standard deviations 80 and 20 CU, or 8% and 2% of initial total wealth. They are not 8% and 2% of the 800-CU liquid sleeve. The objective mean is M(a) = 1.08x + 1.03y + (1.042 + a)z + g(gc − 140) + 320 − 40. Since ∂M/∂a = z ≥ 0 and variance is fixed with respect to a, the worst score is at a = 0. The board's robustness choice has a clear derivation; the interval itself remains a judgment.

    The grid contains (400/25 + 1)(500/25 + 1)(150/25 + 1) = 2,499 candidates, of which 670 are feasible. Enumeration checks the full budget, position caps, lot restrictions, V ≤ 6400, active variance ≤ 400, maximum date-1 bill plus buffer, and each design reserve. The rejection totals are nonexclusive. Sorting all feasible rows with the declared tie rule is a global certificate for this finite problem; a first-order condition from an unconstrained continuous problem would not establish the answer.

If insufficient sale capacity prevents even the call and grant, subsequent private rights are unspecified; the model reports payment failure and null for unsupported later cash/reserve. It does not assume a free waiver or a particular default recovery.

  6. Authorized partial fill and the terminal-wealth identity

    The target sells 100 B and buys 75 E. The desk can first sell only 75 B, leaving B = 275. Completing the intended equity order would produce (325,275,0), pay 0.375 + 0.150 = 0.525 in fees and leave cash 199.475. After the high design bill, cash is 199.475 × 1.005 − 200 = 0.472375. This plan can pay the bill but fails the 20-CU buffer by 19.527625. Its total variance 6315.76 and active variance 394/3 pass their limits; variance compliance does not imply liquidity compliance.

    The continuation rule fixes B = 275 and z = 0 and restricts E to the authorized 250–325 range. The best feasible grid point is (300,275,0). It buys only 50 E after the actual sale, pays 0.25 + 0.15 = 0.4 and leaves cash 224.6. The maximum design bill then leaves 25.723; design reserves are 777.151615 and 708.351615. There are 25 unfilled B sale units and 25 canceled E purchase units. The target and benchmark remain unchanged. No previously executed equity purchase needs reversal and no fee is erased.

    The E factor is 1.04 × 0.98 × 1.03 × 1.01 = 1.06027376 and B factor is 1.01 × 1 × 0.98 × 1.015 = 1.004647. The nominal counterfactual uses K's factor 0.96921216 and finishes with 940.688207875 CU. This is a disclosed counterfactual; the board cannot claim it was the original robust policy or infer which policy will win in future from one path.

    Target − benchmark = 3.557795125 CU.
    Actual − target = −1.213914625 CU.
    Actual − benchmark = 2.3438805 CU = 3.557795125 − 1.213914625.

    Both unfilled legs matter. Missing 25 E while retaining 25 B gives target-minus-actual return opportunity 25(GE − GB) = 1.390669 CU. The actual portfolio saved 0.175 in initial fees, which becomes 0.176754375 at date 2. Hence target minus actual equals 1.390669 − 0.176754375 = 1.213914625. Comparing only filled trades, or charging target fees to actual without disclosure, breaks this identity.

    More generally, for target holdings t and actual h at initial price one, let Δ = t − h, terminal factors G and fees Kt, Kh. Since ct − ch = −ΣΔ + Kh − Kt, target minus actual terminal wealth is ΣΔ(G − 1) + (Kh − Kt)g² + (ΣΔ)(1 − g²). The last term is zero here because the two missing notionals offset. This derivation preserves cash's foregone accrual and every unfilled target leg; it does not assume a displayed quote guarantees execution.

    A terminal reserve is not a total-pool return. The private call transfers money within the pool, whereas scholarships are external flows. Independent private values at external-flow boundaries are absent, so a total-pool TWR cannot be recovered by pretending the private carrying value remained constant. The matched portfolios nevertheless have the same dated external obligations and private rights, making their terminal-wealth difference informative. It measures a realized policy comparison, not proof of managerial skill, an equilibrium alpha or a causal performance effect.

  7. An acceptable IPS and decision memo

    A defensible benchmark recommendation adopts the robust target (325,250,0), retains K as the screened manager for further diligence, authorizes the specified staged-order fallback and keeps the strategic benchmark fixed. The board deliberately trades a small upper-overlay score advantage for a better minimum score under its interval. The memo should acknowledge the thin risk margin of the nominal alternative and the robust policy's small design-stress reserve headroom. The outside-design stress is a genuine residual vulnerability; a positive ordinary expected reserve is not a promise to meet every possible grant.

    The IPS should identify scholarship beneficiaries, the existing private obligation, a one-year decision horizon and its half-year cash bottleneck. Assign the board responsibility for objectives, ambiguity interval, risk limits, benchmark and any donor support; the investment staff for the vintage/evidence register and independent model; the treasury function for payment-date cash; the desk for bond-sale-first execution within the authorized continuation rule; and an independent reviewer for recomputing results and reporting exceptions. These are proposed case governance roles, not legal obligations. The dated institutional IPS reference supports connecting objectives, responsibilities, liquidity, benchmarks and monitoring; the numerical limits and recommendation are original choices.

    Before releasing the equity order, treasury verifies actual settled sale proceeds and recomputes every remaining constraint. At each payment date it confirms the private call notice, grant amount, liquid buffer and sale authority. Risk monitoring uses current exposures and reports both total and active risk, with a record of whether covariance changes are new planning assumptions or genuine new evidence. Performance reporting retains the January target, the authorized actual holdings, the fixed benchmark, the period/vintage labels, fees and unfilled orders. A changed limit, manager forecast, private sale right, donor commitment or new contingency requires a dated decision; the report preserves the old policy for attribution.

    At least five concrete evidence requests should connect uncertainty to action. Examples: obtain timestamped manager records and revision controls to assess the selection history; reconcile fee bases and net performance to cash records before comparing managers; obtain a longer unselected sample and a truly prospective research protocol before increasing the overlay; inspect private capital-call rights and notice periods before approving the buffer; obtain executable bond liquidity/fee terms and settlement timing before increasing trade size; verify private distributions and valuation independence before presenting a whole-pool return; examine how risk choices change across defensible priors and residual covariances before adopting a higher risk budget. Generic requests to “do more research” earn little credit.

    Full judgment credit does not require professing certainty in γ = 4 or a 700-CU reserve floor. A learner may recommend a more conservative policy, a smaller private commitment at a future contractual opportunity, or negotiating additional support. They must first reproduce the assigned optimum, price the recommendation's opportunity costs under stated assumptions, identify the authority and funds it requires, and show what cannot currently be changed. They must not claim the existing private stake is readily liquid merely because a recommendation needs cash.

    For a five-minute defense, require the learner to trace one observation from release to decision, one covariance term from common factor to total wealth, and one sale from original units to reduced future proceeds. An instructor may withhold the reference output until the independent submission is fixed. Evidence of reasoning, honest uncertainty and reconciled cash earns credit; a polished presentation does not compensate for an unavailable input or an unfunded commitment.

  8. Interventions, teach-back and delayed retention

    Intervention group A — Separate information from forecast. On a copy, move M's period-4 second-vintage release to 2 January 2025, leaving every other input unchanged. Separately, restore the baseline and add 0.10 to K's gross held-out period-5 return. Predict which research, allocation and reporting fields should change before running either copy. Then explain why these are counterfactual tests rather than evidence for revising a completed historical decision.

    Answer. Early release makes M's January net active mean 0.008, so M is selected. Index covariance, supplied selected-manager loadings/means/residual risk, feasibility and optimal exposure quantities remain unchanged: robust (325,250,0), nominal (325,225,25). The nominal counterfactual now uses M's held-out factor and ends at 7543884431/8000000 = 942.985553875 CU; baseline robust and actual hold no manager, so their outcomes are unchanged. The second edit leaves selection, training risk, both optimal portfolios and the strategic benchmark unchanged. It changes K's evaluation and the nominal counterfactual to 7545697583/8000000 = 943.212197875 CU. A model that changes its January allocation because only a held-out return changed has leaked future information. The supplied forward forecast applies to whichever manager wins the stated screen; it is deliberately a separate policy assumption, not an automatic estimate from that manager's history.

    Intervention group B — Separate preference and execution. Set the overlay upper bound to zero, keeping its lower bound zero. Separately restore the baseline and increase executable initial bond-sale capacity to 100. Explain the optimal-policy and realized-report changes without modifying the benchmark. As an optional independent transfer, raise γ to 6 while keeping all limits fixed.

    Answer. With a singleton overlay interval, robust and nominal objectives coincide and both select (325,250,0); the 670-position feasible set is unchanged. Full bond capacity allows the original sale of 100 and purchase of 75 E. Actual holdings equal target, actual entry cost is 0.575, the two unfilled legs and implementation gap vanish, and actual reserve becomes 941.725582625. The strategic benchmark remains 938.1677875. If γ rises to 6, the robust optimum moves to (250,325,0) and nominal to (250,300,25); greater variance aversion changes the objective rather than retroactively altering observed returns. Each edit belongs in a preserved change log.

    Intervention group C — Distinguish paying a bill from passing policy. Restore baseline inputs. Reduce outside-design bond-sale capacity first to 20 and then to zero. Reconcile cash, payment status and the residual policy failure. State why the reference should not invent a recovery value after actual nonpayment.

    Answer. At capacity 20 the sale raises 19.16, pays the 240-CU call/grant bill and leaves 4.707125. The 20-CU buffer is short by 15.292875. Terminal reserve is 876369057/1600000 = 547.730660625, below the floor by 152.269339375. This is an available continuation with failed buffer and floor tests. At zero capacity the scheduled payment gap is 115623/8000 = 14.452875. The model reports payments_funded: false and null for subsequent cash and reserve because no default/waiver terms are supplied. Keeping the original private payoff after not meeting its call would assume an unprovided right. None of these outside-design changes may rewrite the approved target or ordinary realized report.

    Teach-back prompt. Explain, without code, how the same case can have K win the research screen, receive no robust allocation, and show an actual portfolio outperforming its strategic benchmark even though execution reduced wealth relative to target.

    Model answer. The screen compares four available historical net active observations and selects K. The allocation uses a separate forward covariance/mean model, costs, private funding, constraints and a lower-overlay preference; those premises lead to z = 0. Actual minus benchmark is positive 2.3438805, but this decomposes into target policy advantage 3.557795125 and implementation loss −1.213914625. The benchmarks answer different questions and the final path cannot identify skill. Passing requires those three mechanisms, their units and the unchanged dates/benchmark; merely naming “risk” or “luck” is insufficient.

    Delayed retention, after 7–14 days. Reconstruct three arguments from the original inputs without looking at the solution: (i) why CX remains in the cohort but not the allocation menu; (ii) why the private claim cancels from active variance but not total variance; (iii) why a forced sale's terminal effect is not merely its spread and fee.

    Answers and criteria. (i) The initial cohort is fixed before the liquidation; 0.7644 survives and then earns zero, but a liquidated vehicle cannot take a new mandate. State both population and cash treatment. (ii) The target and benchmark own the identical random payoff, so subtraction cancels it; total wealth still carries its factor covariance and residual variance. State both the common-claim condition and retained total-risk terms. (iii) Selling q original units raises net cash after costs, changes subsequent cash accrual and removes q times the bond's terminal gross payoff. State all three effects and the bill date. Require all three complete explanations, then change one fact—different benchmark private ownership, a later call, or a reduced sale cap—and ask which identity or constraint must be rebuilt.

What the completed project establishes

The deliverable establishes that the learner can audit a dated synthetic record, implement a transparent bounded policy, conserve cash and claims, and defend the limits of an inference. It does not validate actual manager skill, the board's risk preferences, a traded private valuation or compliance with a performance standard. The next extension is a prospectively specified study with real accessible data, complete inclusion rules, appropriate uncertainty analysis and independent review. Preserve these same information, funding and reporting disciplines when the data become larger.

Oral transfer and teach-back

Allow 20 minutes after the written examination and project. The examiner may display the numerical facts below, but the learner should explain the mechanism without notes. Four prompts are worth five points each; require at least 17/20 and no unresolved critical error. Per prompt award two points for correct economic and quantitative reasoning, one for the relevant constraint or information date, one for an explicit assumption or boundary, and one for a clear answer that distinguishes a calculation from an evidence claim. Follow-up changes should be disclosed prospectively rather than introduced into an earlier information set.

  1. A liability changes the action menu. At a decision node, liquid wealth is 10 CU. Safe wealth has terminal gross return one. A risky investment has gross returns 1.6 and 0.8 with equal conditional probabilities. A terminal liability of 9 must be paid. Available risky fractions are 0, 0.1, 0.5 and 1; there is no intermediate trade or borrowing. The objective is expected log of terminal surplus, which must be strictly positive in each possible state. Which action is best? How does the choice change if a guaranteed additional CU arrives at the terminal date before the liability? Explain why terminal income may alter this node's choice but cannot be used to pay an earlier bill.
  2. Equal expected payoff is not equal price. Physical state probabilities are (0.75, 0.25), and a strictly positive stochastic discount factor is (0.8, 1.4). Price claims X = (1, 0) and Y = (0, 3). They have the same physical expected payoff. Explain the price difference and identify the safe bond's price and the distinction between physical and normalized pricing probabilities.
  3. Design evidence that could disappoint you. A manager presents the best strategy found among 100 historical rules, a positive net information ratio, and a benchmark chosen after inspecting its worst quarter. Describe a prospective evaluation that could credibly reject the manager's skill claim. Address the information cutoff, strategy search, original opportunity set, fees and benchmark, and the uncertainty remaining after a successful test.
  4. Infeasibility is a possible result. Cash is 20 CU, a capital call of 18 CU and a grant payment of five CU are both due today. The cash floor afterward is four. A locked private asset has NAV 60 but cannot be sold or pledged today. A liquid bond can be sold at 0.95 CU per unit, without other costs, but the authorized sale cap is seven units. No credit facility exists. Can the specified plan be authorized as feasible? Quantify the gap after the largest permitted sale and describe what evidence an actual repair would require.
Oral benchmarks and transfer boundaries
  1. Without the extra income, surplus for risky fraction w is (1 + 6w, 1 − 2w). Fractions 0.5 and 1 violate strict positivity. Fractions zero and 0.1 have surplus products 1 and 1.28, respectively, so 0.1 maximizes 0.5 ln(product) over the given menu. With one extra CU arriving before payment, surplus becomes (2 + 6w, 2 − 2w). Products for 0, 0.1 and 0.5 are 4, 4.68 and 5; fraction one has zero bad-state surplus and is inadmissible. Now 0.5 is optimal within this menu. A node-specific continuation decision conditions on information then observed; this finite menu does not establish the optimum over all real fractions. Terminal resources enter terminal surplus, not an earlier cash account. This is a transfer of liability-aware contingent choice, with the log domain enforced before comparing objectives.
  2. State prices are q = p m = (0.60, 0.35). X costs 0.60 CU and Y costs 1.05 CU, although both have physical expected payoff 0.75 CU. Y delivers in the state with the larger discount factor, where marginal valuation is higher in this representation. A unit safe bond costs 0.60 + 0.35 = 0.95. Normalized pricing probabilities are (12/19, 7/19), not physical probabilities (3/4, 1/4); discounting a physical expected payoff at the safe rate would not price both claims. A positive SDF gives this linear valuation for the specified claims; it does not by itself identify an investor's utility or prove a unique SDF in a general incomplete market. Review state prices and discount factors.
  3. Freeze the strategy and all formation rules using a documented cutoff; retain the 100-rule search history and an independently dated evaluation period. Define a feasible benchmark before seeing evaluation returns, including exposure/currency/cash conventions. Preserve the original eligible cohort, failed funds and delisting recoveries; record availability dates and revisions. Reconcile gross returns to realized fees and execution costs, and specify an uncertainty analysis appropriate to the sampling dependence and selection claim. A weak or negative fresh net result is allowed to overturn the claim; redefining the strategy or benchmark after the result starts a new experiment. A positive evaluation remains conditional on risk controls, sampling assumptions, persistence and implementability. It does not establish causality or guaranteed future alpha. Other defensible designs earn credit when they make these same claims falsifiable. Review factor exposures, joint hypotheses and search and performance evaluation.
  4. The required sale proceeds are 18 + 5 + 4 − 20 = 7 CU. Seven units generate only 6.65, leaving cash 3.65 and a reserve gap 0.35. The locked NAV supplies no today's cash. Without the cap, a sale of 7/0.95 = 140/19 ≈ 7.3684 units would suffice; it is not permitted under the stated policy. A repair needs documented authority and timely resources: for example an actual pre-deadline cash contribution of 0.35, or an authorized, executable change in the sale cap. A hoped-for waiver, renegotiated grant or loan cannot be booked as though it already exists. Preserve the failure and escalation record. Review illiquidity and policy implementation.

After the oral, write a short correction memo: the original claim, the failed assumption or calculation, the changed decision and one fresh test. A polished explanation without a valid cash or probability calculation does not repair the underlying domain error.

Delayed retention assessment

Two to four weeks later, allow 90 minutes, closed-book with a basic calculator. These six new items are worth ten points each, for 60 overall. Require at least 51/60 and at least eight on every item. They deliberately join chapter boundaries; a correct isolated formula is insufficient. Use the same carry-forward and critical-error rules as the written examinations. Do not use these cases as additional observations in the project's holdout sample.

  1. Returns and a constrained risk minimum. An account starts at 1,000 CU, earns 8% in year 1, then immediately receives an external contribution of 200. Year 2 earns −5% before a fixed 16-CU ending fee, paid from the account. Compute ending wealth, the net two-year time-weighted return and the annual money-weighted IRR for this contribution history; explain why the last two differ. In a separate prospective two-asset allocation, variances are 0.04 and 0.01 and covariance is 0.005. Fully invest without shorts, with asset-A weight at least 0.20. Derive the minimum-variance weight and portfolio variance; identify the unconstrained minimum too.
  2. A bound is not an equilibrium forecast. There are three possible terminal states with physical probabilities (0.20, 0.50, 0.30). A unit safe bond costs 0.95 CU. Asset A costs one CU and pays (0, 1, 2). Signed frictionless trading is allowed. Parameterize all strictly positive state-price vectors matching both prices and derive the open arbitrage-free price interval for claim X = (1, 0, 1). Exhibit the arbitrage if X instead costs the lower endpoint. Separately, a proposed CAPM representation assigns A beta 1.4 and the market an expected excess return of 5%. Compare its required return with A's physical expected return using the safe rate implied by the bond. Explain whether a discrepancy alone supplies an arbitrage.
  3. An omitted exposure and an apparent winner. Four equally weighted observations have traded factor excess returns F = (−2, −1, 1, 2)% and G = (1.5, −0.5, −0.5, 1.5)%. A strategy's excess returns are Y = (0, −2.5, 0.5, 6)%. Treat these as a finite descriptive dataset. Fit Y on an intercept and F, then explain what changes when G is included. A benchmark of 1.5F was fixed before evaluation. Compute the gross and net information ratios using population moments over these four observations; the strategy pays a constant fee of 0.4 percentage points per observation and the benchmark does not. Explain why discovering this strategy as the best of 100 rules on these same observations does not demonstrate persistent skill.
  4. Nontraded income changes the hedge. Initial liquid wealth is 10 CU. Investing x CU in a risky asset produces terminal gross returns 1.4 in boom and 0.8 in slump; the remainder earns gross one. Each state has probability one-half. Nontraded terminal income is (2, 6) CU and a fixed five-CU liability is paid after income arrives. Maximize E[S] − (λ/2) Var(S), where S is terminal surplus, λ = 1 CU−1, and 0 ≤ x ≤ 10. Derive the optimum, state surpluses and variance. Recompute the optimum with no nontraded income and explain the direction of the change. Do not treat the nontraded income as money available to buy assets initially.
  5. Appraisal risk and payable cash. A pool has 50 CU cash before day 10. A capital call of 30 and a grant payment of 12 are due that day; its closing cash floor is ten. A private holding has reported NAV 100 but cannot be sold or pledged before month 12. In a joint stress an additional eight-CU margin payment is due on day 10. A separate liquid bond can be sold on day 10 for 0.98 CU per unit, without fees, up to twelve divisible units. Calculate the base and joint-stress funding gaps and the minimum stress sale. If capacity falls to ten units, is the stress plan feasible? Separately, an appraisal series obeys at = 0.6at−1 + 0.4ut; the prior appraisal return is 2% and the current one −2%. Recover the latent current return. Under stationary iid latent returns, derive the appraisal-to-latent variance ratio and state why this stylized unsmoothing does not create a liquid sale price.
  6. Measure the original target and fund the policy. The decision is to sell 200 shares at a decision benchmark of 40 CU per share. Only 120 sell, at average price 39.50; explicit fees total six CU. The remaining 80 shares are marked at 39 at the horizon. There are no other positions, flows or initial cash. Compute whole-target implementation shortfall and its filled and unfilled components. The arrival midpoint for the fills was 39.80; compute the signed effective spread per filled share, excluding fees. A prospective cash floor of 5,000 CU must now be met. Additional shares can be sold immediately at 39, with a fee of 0.05 per share, in whole shares and with capacity for all 80. Find the minimum additional sale, resulting cash and whether that repair completes the original mandate. Explain how to report the repair without rewriting the decision benchmark.
Delayed solutions, full reasoning and ten-point scoring
  1. The first valuation is 1,080; after the contribution, 1,280 enters year 2. Gross ending assets are 1,280 × 0.95 = 1,216; the fee leaves 1,200 CU. The net second-period factor is 1,200/1,280 = 0.9375. Linking the two flow-separated factors gives 1.08 × 0.9375 − 1 = 0.0125, or 1.25% net over two years. The annual money-weighted equation is −1,000 − 200/(1+i) + 1,200/(1+i)² = 0. Its economically admissible root is i = 0; the other gross-factor root is −1.2, outside 1+i > 0. More money was invested in the losing second period, so a positive linked return can coexist with zero total cash profit and zero IRR. Compare annual rates consistently: annualizing the TWR gives √1.0125 − 1, still positive, whereas the annual IRR is zero; the two-year TWR and annual IRR have different reporting horizons. For the separate allocation, v(w) = 0.04w² + 0.01(1−w)² + 0.01w(1−w) = 0.01 − 0.01w + 0.04w². Thus v′ = −0.01 + 0.08w, with unconstrained minimum w = 1/8 and variance 0.009375. On [0.20,1], variance is increasing from the lower endpoint; the constrained minimum is w = 0.20, variance 0.0096. Credit: dated ending wealth and fee treatment 2; net TWR 1; IRR and difference 2; covariance quadratic 2; both optima with justification 2; constrained variance 1. Repair returns, covariance and constraints.
  2. The restrictions are q₁ + q₂ + q₃ = 0.95 and q₂ + 2q₃ = 1. Write q = (t, 0.90−2t, 0.05+t), where strict positivity is equivalent to 0 < t < 0.45. X therefore has price q₁ + q₃ = 0.05 + 2t, ranging over (0.05,0.95). Every interior price supplies a strictly positive pricing vector for the extended market. At price 0.05, buy X, short one A and buy one bond. Initial cost is 0.05 − 1 + 0.95 = 0, with payoff (2,0,0): an arbitrage because the first state is possible. The bond implies rf = 1/0.95 − 1 = 1/19 ≈ 5.2632%. A's physical expected payoff is 0.5 + 0.3 × 2 = 1.1, so its expected return is 10%. Proposed CAPM required return is 1/19 + 1.4(0.05) ≈ 12.2632%, a discrepancy of −2.2632 percentage points. That rejects joint compatibility of the supplied moments/beta and proposed CAPM restrictions, not the existence of positive state prices. A factor-model discrepancy is not itself a statewise arbitrage. Credit: pricing family and positivity 3; interval and endpoint trade 3; safe and expected returns 2; CAPM comparison and implication 2. Repair equilibrium restrictions and incomplete-market pricing.
  3. In percentage-point units, E[F] = 0, Var(F) = 2.5, E[G] = 0.5, Var(G) = 1 and Cov(F,G) = 0. The exact identity is Y = 1.5F + 2G. The one-factor projection has slope 1.5 and intercept one percentage point, with residual 2(G−0.5). Adding G gives slopes 1.5 and 2, zero intercept and zero residual in this dataset. Relative to the fixed 1.5F benchmark, gross active returns are (3,−1,−1,3)%, mean 1% and population tracking error 2%; gross IR is 0.5. The constant fee changes the mean to 0.6% without changing the descriptive tracking error, yielding net IR 0.3. Relative to the full two-factor fitted identity, the net intercept is −0.4 percentage points. An omitted exposure with a nonzero sample mean can explain a one-factor intercept; a selected four-observation fit cannot identify future skill or validate the pricing of either factor. Freeze a feasible future benchmark, preserve the search and original cohort, and evaluate fresh net outcomes with stated uncertainty and dependence assumptions. Credit: one-factor moments/coefficients 2; exact two-factor identity and interpretation 2; gross IR 2; net IR and fee effect 2; selection/evidence distinction 2. Repair factor construction, search and joint hypotheses and net performance.
  4. Terminal surplus is S = (7 + 0.4x, 11 − 0.2x) CU. Hence E[S] = 9 + 0.1x and Var(S) = (−2 + 0.3x)² CU². With the specified units for λ, the objective's derivative is 0.7 − 0.09x; its second derivative is −0.09, so the interior maximizer is x = 70/9 ≈ 7.7778 CU. Surplus is (91/9,85/9) CU, mean 88/9 and variance 1/9 CU². With no nontraded income, surplus is (5 + 0.4x, 5 − 0.2x), mean 5 + 0.1x and variance 0.09x²; the optimum falls to x = 10/9 ≈ 1.1111. The original countercyclical income insures the low risky-return state, allowing larger liquid risky exposure under this surplus objective. Both optima lie within the actual ten-CU initial budget; neither capitalizes the nontraded receipt into cash available today. Credit: dated surplus 2; mean/variance/objective 2; first optimum and concavity 2; state outcomes/variance 1; no-income optimum 2; hedge and budget explanation 1. Repair strategic allocation.
  5. Base closing cash before a sale is 50 − 30 − 12 = 8, two below the floor. With the extra margin payment it is zero, ten below the floor. The minimum stress sale is 10/0.98 = 500/49 ≈ 10.2041 units, within capacity twelve, leaving exactly ten CU cash. With capacity ten the largest proceeds are 9.80; the reserve still fails by 0.20. The locked NAV cannot cure either date-10 gap. Unsmoothing gives ut = (−0.02 − 0.6 × 0.02)/0.4 = −0.08, or −8%. If latent returns are iid with finite variance and the filter is stationary, Var(a) = 0.6² Var(a) + 0.4² Var(u), so Var(a)/Var(u) = 0.16/0.64 = 1/4; reported volatility is half latent volatility in that model. Serially correlated latent returns, changing appraisal coefficients or a nonstationary start invalidate that variance shortcut. Unsmoothing changes a statistical estimate, not redemption terms or executable bids. Credit: two gaps 2; minimum sale and cash reconciliation 2; restricted-capacity conclusion 1; recovered return 2; variance derivation 2; liquidity/model boundary 1. Repair alternative assets and execution capacity.
  6. The paper target would produce 200 × 40 = 8,000 CU. Actual wealth at the horizon is 120 × 39.50 − 6 + 80 × 39 = 7,854; shortfall is 146 CU. Filled cost is 120(40−39.50) + 6 = 66; opportunity cost on the remaining shares is 80(40−39) = 80. With sell sign s = −1, effective spread excluding fees is 2s(P−M) = 2(−1)(39.50−39.80) = 0.60 CU per filled share. Cash before repair is 4,734 CU. Each additional share supplies 39 − 0.05 = 38.95, so the required integer sale is ceil[(5,000−4,734)/38.95] = 7. Six would leave 4,967.70; seven leave 5,006.65 and 73 shares. That sale repairs the cash floor, not the original all-200-share completion target. Its additional 0.35-CU fee also reduces wealth if the same 39 mark is retained. Keep the original decision price, original 200-share target, partial-fill shortfall, new instruction time, extra fee and residual risk visible. An authorized prospective change can alter the future mandate but cannot erase its earlier execution history. Credit: total and two-component shortfall 4; signed spread 2; minimum integer repair/cash 2; remaining target and honest reporting 2. Repair signed trading costs and policy reporting.

Notation index

Symbols have local definitions; a factor premium, a price and a cash amount are not interchangeable merely because each is written as a number. Rates below are decimals unless percentage-point units are explicitly stated.

Concept index and targeted remediation

Chapter and conceptual distinctionAssessment routeEvidence of repair
1. Returns and opportunity sets: investment return versus external funding.Q1 in each form; retention 1.Reconstruct valuation immediately before and after every contribution and fee.
2. Diversification: covariance versus a list of standalone volatilities.Q1; diagnostic 2; retention 1.Build portfolio state returns and reconcile their variance with the quadratic form.
3. Optimization: a stationary formula versus a feasible optimum.Q1; diagnostic 5; retention 1.Check boundary directions and repeat the choice under changed expected returns or covariance.
4. CAPM: an equilibrium restriction versus an arbitrary proxy regression.Q2; retention 2.Name the market, expectations and trading assumptions required for the claimed premium.
5. State prices: unique replication versus a range of admissible prices.Q2; oral 2; retention 2.Check every pricing equation and positivity; construct a statewise trade at an invalid endpoint.
6. Factors: fitted exposures versus priced and executable factor claims.Q3; retention 3; project.Show what an added exposure changes and identify residual risk and any untested pricing restriction.
7. Efficiency and behavior: an anomaly versus a joint, selected test.Q3; oral 3; project.Freeze the information set and strategy search; identify evidence that would overturn the explanation.
8. Active management: gross fit versus prospective net benchmark-relative evidence.Q3; retention 3; project.Reconcile fees, cohort membership, benchmark exposure, active mean and tracking error.
9. Intertemporal allocation: a static weight versus a liability-aware contingent policy.Q4; oral 1; retention 4.State the objective and available actions at each information node; verify surplus and budget domains.
10. Alternatives: appraisal wealth versus dated liquidity.Q4; retention 5; project.Fund gross payments before netting later distributions; report unsmoothing assumptions separately.
11. Execution: filled-price quality versus whole-target implementation.Q5; retention 6; project.Conserve signed cash and holdings, retain unfilled quantities, and check actual executable capacity.
12. Investment policy: an attractive allocation versus an authorized, reportable mandate.Q5; oral 4; project.Reject infeasible policies, identify decision rights and preserve original benchmarks through exceptions.

From investment theory to accountable decisions

Investment analysis links three different questions. What does a security pay, and when? Which prices or expected returns are compatible with stated trading and equilibrium assumptions? Which feasible policy should this investor choose, given liabilities, information, costs and governance? A replication answers a pricing question under its trading assumptions. A sample regression describes a dataset. An allocation solves a stated objective. None alone establishes the other conclusions.

The volume's project makes those connections inspectable through a frozen research history, a funded policy and a prospective comparator. The transferable habit is to preserve the chain from information to decision to execution to evaluation, including the cases in which the answer is infeasible or inconclusive. Advanced instruments in Volume 10, institutional balance sheets in Volume 11 and advanced inference in Volume 12 extend that chain; these links identify successor specifications and do not imply unwritten material is available. The source routes in the twelve accepted chapters support the methods used here; the assessment's cases, data, scoring and transfer questions are author-created.
